title: Can Chevron Build a Lithium Business in the Smackover Formation? - TradingView
content: Chevron Corporation CVX entered the U.S. lithium sector in June 2025, when it announced two leasehold acquisitions in the Smackover Formation in Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas. The company initially put the combined position at about 125,000 net acres and later revised that figure to about 135,000 net acres. Chevron acquired the leases to find out whether it can produce lithium from salty water found deep underground. The company is pursuing lithium mainly for energy storage, including batteries used in electric vehicles and on the power grid. Chevron is assessing the underground resource, testing direct lithium extraction and designing the facilities it would need. The process separates lithium from salty water pumped to the surface, then returns the remaining water to the underground reservoir. That work draws on skills Chevron already uses in its oil and gas business, from assessing reservoirs to drilling wells and handling fluids. The company is also refining its product specifications so it can discuss with potential customers what they need and what the project might eventually be able to supply. Chevron plans to develop the acreage in phases and adjust the pace to market conditions. The company has yet to announce when commercial production might start or how much lithium it aims to produce. Oil and gas production still drives most of Chevron’s earnings, so the near-term question for investors is what the extraction tests reveal about the project’s economics. How much lithium Chevron can recover from the brine, and what it costs to recover it, will help determine whether the acreage can support a profitable business. A U.S. lithium supply chain depends on producers being able to meet battery makers’ quality standards consistently. Producing battery-grade lithium in small batches is an early step. The next test is whether that quality holds as output increases. ExxonMobil Holdings XOM holds brine rights across more than 300,000 net acres in the Smackover Formation. ExxonMobil has produced battery-grade lithium carbonate at its Texas pilot facility using brine from southern Arkansas. ExxonMobil’s preliminary agreement with LG Chem for a potential lithium supply deal is nonbinding. The company aims to produce enough lithium for about one million electric vehicles a year by the first half of the 2030s. Occidental Petroleum OXY is testing direct lithium extraction in California’s Imperial Valley through a joint venture with BHE Renewables. Occidental’s TerraLithium subsidiary and its partner produced battery-grade lithium carbonate from geothermal brine and converted lithium chloride into lithium hydroxide in separate tests. Occidental and its partner expect demonstration operations to continue through 2027 as they assess whether the process is economically viable at commercial scale. title: CVX vs. SHEL: Which Energy Giant Offers Better Shareholder Returns? - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron CorporationCVX and Shell plc SHEL continue to prioritize shareholder rewards through dividends and share repurchases, supported by strong cash generation and disciplined capital allocation. Both energy giants reported robust third-quarter 2026 results despite volatile commodity prices and geopolitical uncertainties. Chevron returned approximately $6 billion to its shareholders during the quarter, while Shell distributed $5.3 billion and announced a fresh $5 billion share repurchase program. However, their contrasting dividend policies, buyback strategies and earnings outlooks raise an important question: Which energy major offers better shareholder returns? Let's examine their fundamentals, stock performance and earnings expectations to determine which company holds the edge. Chevron has demonstrated stronger share-price momentum than Shell over the past year. CVX’s shares gained 39.1%, outperforming SHEL's 27.8% increase by 11.3 percentage points. Both stocks experienced considerable volatility during the period, particularly around midyear, before recovering in subsequent months. Chevron maintained its performance advantage despite fluctuations in energy markets. Chevron's shareholder-friendly capital allocation strategy remains a key investment attraction. During the third quarter, the company paid approximately $3.5 billion in dividends and repurchased $2.5 billion of shares. Chevron declared a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share, supported by 39 consecutive years of annual dividend increases. Management continues prioritizing dividend growth, efficient capital investments and balance-sheet strength. Shell also maintained substantial shareholder distributions, paying approximately $2.2 billion in dividends and repurchasing $3.2 billion of shares during the quarter. The company declared a quarterly dividend of 39.06 cents per ordinary share, compared with 35.80 cents in the year-ago period. Chevron's established dividend growth record offers greater visibility for income-oriented investors. Shell's higher allocation toward repurchases, meanwhile, reflects a more buyback-focused shareholder return strategy. Overall, Chevron holds the advantage in dividend consistency, while Shell demonstrates stronger near-term repurchase momentum. Shell's share repurchase strategy remains a major differentiator in its capital allocation approach. Following approximately $3.2 billion in third-quarter buybacks, Shell announced a new $5 billion repurchase program, expected to conclude by its fourth-quarter 2026 earnings announcement. The initiative reflects management's confidence in the company's cash-generating capabilities and commitment to returning surplus capital to its shareholders. Chevron, meanwhile, maintained quarterly repurchases of approximately $2.5 billion. Management reiterated its intended quarterly buyback range of $2.5 billion to $3 billion. Shell's larger newly announced program provides greater near-term buyback potential, while Chevron's established framework supports distribution predictability. However, the ultimate benefits of repurchases depend on execution and the valuations at which shares are acquired. Strong cash generation remains essential for sustaining shareholder rewards through fluctuating commodity-price environments. Chevron generated $16 billion in operating cash flow and $12 billion in free cash flow during third-quarter 2026. Adjusted earnings totaled $10.4 billion, supported by improved refining margins and operational efficiency. Shell generated approximately $21 billion in operating cash flow, $16.3 billion in free cash flow and $10.8 billion in adjusted earnings. Shell's stronger absolute cash generation provides considerable flexibility to finance shareholder distributions and future investments. However, the companies use different free cash flow definitions, limiting direct comparability. Chevron's net debt-to-operating-cash-flow ratio stood at 0.4 times, reflecting a robust financial position. Meanwhile, Shell's gearing improved to 16.6% from 18.7% sequentially, demonstrating strengthening balance-sheet flexibility. Both companies appear financially positioned to sustain shareholder distributions, although weaker commodity prices and elevated capital requirements could affect future cash flows. Positive earnings estimate revisions provide additional insights into the companies' profitability outlooks. Over the past 60 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for Chevron's 2026 earnings increased 13.26%, from $16.52 to $18.71 per share. Its 2027 estimate climbed 22.49%, from $14.67 to $17.97 per share. For Shell, the consensus estimate for 2026 earnings increased 15.52%, from $10.89 to $12.58 per share. Meanwhile, its 2027 estimate rose 12.14%, from $10.13 to $11.36 per share. Shell demonstrated stronger upward revisions for 2026, while Chevron recorded greater improvement in 2027 expectations. This suggests comparatively stronger longer-term earnings revision momentum for Chevron. Both Chevron and Shell offer attractive shareholder return opportunities. Shell stands out for stronger absolute cash generation and aggressive share repurchases, while Chevron benefits from consistent dividend growth, superior historical share-price performance and improving longer-term earnings expectations. Chevron's 39.1% share-price gain, 39-year dividend growth streak, robust balance sheet and stronger 2027 earnings estimate revisions collectively reinforce its investment appeal. Although both stocks carry a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), Chevron emerges as the better pick for investors prioritizing consistent shareholder returns and longer-term earnings momentum. Shell remains an appealing alternative for investors emphasizing buybacks and cash generation. title: Chevron vs. Occidental Petroleum: Which Energy Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027? - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron maintains a diversified global footprint with operations spanning crude oil production, refining, and chemical manufacturing. Occidental Petroleum focuses on high-production basins and is aggressively expanding its carbon management and low-carbon technology capabilities. Which energy heavyweight offers the best path for your portfolio through 2027? The energy landscape is evolving as traditional oil producers balance output with shifting climate policies. Investors deciding between Chevron(NYSE:CVX)and Occidental Petroleum(NYSE:OXY)must choose between a diversified giant and a specialized producer. Chevron provides a traditional integrated model, controlling everything from extraction to retail fuel sales. Occidental Petroleum focuses on efficiency in specific North American basins while investing in emerging carbon capture technologies. This comparison explores which strategy is better positioned for the next few years. Chevron operates as a global energy leader, producing crude oil and natural gas and refining them into fuels and lubricants sold under brands such as Texaco and Caltex. The company manages a massive supply chain through partnerships such as Chevron Phillips Chemical Company and maintains an interest in Hess Midstream(NYSE:HESM). Its international commitments include nearly 3.2 trillion cubic feet of natural gas primarily from assets in Australia and Israel. In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $225.8 billion, representing a growth rate of roughly 20.8% compared to the prior period. During this time, the company reported a net income of nearly $27.0 billion. These figures highlight the scale of its global operations, though its 11.9% net margin indicates the high costs of maintaining such a broad, integrated network. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.2x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity, showing that the company relies very little on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term debts with current assets, was close to 1.2x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached nearly $16.6 billion, providing significant capital for dividends and reinvestment. Occidental Petroleum focuses heavily on exploration and production, particularly in the Permian and DJ basins. While it remains a fossil fuel leader, it is also positioning itself among renewable energy stocks through its low-carbon ventures business. The company sells oil and natural gas to a wide range of domestic and international refiners while leveraging midstream infrastructure through its equity investment in Western Midstream. In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $25.3 billion, which was a decrease of approximately 4.4% from the previous year. Despite lower revenue, the company achieved a net income of nearly $8.2 billion. This resulted in a net margin of roughly 32.5%, suggesting a highly focused production model that captures significant profit from its specialized asset base. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio reached roughly 0.7x. This indicates a higher reliance on debt than its larger peer, which can increase financial sensitivity during market downturns. The current ratio was approximately 0.9x, showing its current assets were slightly less than its short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was close to $4.1 billion. Chevron faces significant exposure to commodity price volatility, as fluctuations in crude oil and natural gas prices directly impact its earnings. The company must also manage operational risks like severe weather and geopolitical tensions that can disrupt production or lead to asset impairments. Furthermore, the integration of the Hess acquisition entails inherent execution risks, and evolving climate regulations may increase costs for greenhouse gas emissions reductions. Occidental Petroleum contends with volatile global pricing for its primary products, which can limit cash flow during periods of low energy demand. Its higher indebtedness compared to its peers makes it more vulnerable to credit rating downgrades or economic shifts. Additionally, its carbon management initiatives rely on emerging technologies that may not scale as expected, and the company remains involved in a pending tax matter regarding the Anadarko Tronox settlement. Occidental Petroleum currently trades at a lower multiple based on future earnings estimates, while Chevron appears more favorable when comparing market cap to sales over the past 12 months. When comparing Chevron and Occidental, investors should consider a few key factors. Let's have a look at them and see what that tells us about each stock. Firstly, we should consider each company's profitability and balance sheet. Occidental has delivered greater profitability, as measured by its operating margin. The company's operating margin stands at 28.6%, while Chevron's is 16.1%. As for each company's balance sheet, Occidental can also claim a lower amount of net debt. It has $9.1 billion, while Chevron has $20.4 billion. That said, both companies have been aggressively reducing their net debt in recent quarters, with Chevron's total falling from around $40 billion and Occidental's dropping from over $20 billion. Another factor to consider is income potential. Both companies pay a regular dividend. Occidental's current dividend yield is 1.95%, while Chevron's is 3.44%, giving Chevron an edge in the category. Lastly, there's valuation. Since both companies are profitable, we'll examine their respective price-to-earnings (P/E) multiples. Chevron carries a P/E multiple of 15.2x, while Occidental has a P/E multiple of 12.3x. Occidental can claim a modest advantage as its shares are slightly more affordable than Chevron's. To sum up, both of these energy stocks have their strengths. Chevron Corporation CVX is strengthening its upstream growth prospects by advancing offshore oil and gas exploration in Greece. The energy major's latest initiative, undertaken in partnership with Helleniq Energy, marks another step toward expanding its resource base in the Eastern Mediterranean. With Greece seeking to reduce its reliance on imported natural gas, the exploration program offers Chevron an opportunity to identify new hydrocarbon resources and establish additional avenues for long-term production growth. Chevron's entry into Greece complements its established energy operations across the Mediterranean region. In February 2026, the company signed agreements covering four offshore exploration blocks — South Crete 1, South Crete 2, South of Peloponnese and Block A2. Chevron holds a 70% operating interest in the consortium, while Helleniq Energy owns the remaining 30%. The concessions span approximately 47,000 square kilometers, expanding Chevron's exploration portfolio in a region where it already maintains a presence through natural gas projects in Israel, Cyprus and Egypt. The additional acreage provides opportunities to identify commercially attractive resources and support the company's longer-term upstream development strategy. Chevron is moving ahead with seismic surveys in the southern Ionian Sea to assess the hydrocarbon potential of its offshore concessions. Norwegian geophysical company TGS has deployed its Ramform Tethys survey vessel to the region, with operations expected to be completed by the end of January 2027. The surveys will provide valuable subsurface information, allowing Chevron and its partner to evaluate geological formations and identify potential drilling locations. Favorable findings would support decisions on subsequent exploration activities, bringing the company closer to determining whether the acreage contains commercially recoverable resources. Greece's dependence on imported natural gas adds strategic relevance to Chevron's exploration activities. Successful discoveries and subsequent development would provide the country with additional domestic energy supplies while supporting Europe's broader energy security objectives. The project also aligns with Chevron's emphasis on expanding its exploration opportunities through technology and disciplined capital allocation. During its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, management identified the Eastern Mediterranean as a focus area for exploration and highlighted advanced subsurface imaging and artificial intelligence as tools for improving prospect evaluation. For Chevron, the Greek exploration program represents a longer-term growth opportunity rather than an immediate production contributor. While commercial viability remains unproven, favorable seismic results and successful future drilling would strengthen the company's regional resource portfolio and establish another potential source of upstream earnings and cash flows.
